newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: U.N. Council deplores execution, envoy in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council deplores execution, envoy in Kabul.

text.p: United Nations special envoy Norbert Holl flew into Kabul on Sunday for his first meeting with Afghanistan's new Taleban administration as it consolidated its hold on the capital after last week's takeover.

The Islamic militia has paused in its pursuit of forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani, who were apparently regrouping in the Panjshir Valley north of the capital after abandoning Kabul on Friday.

The U.N. Security Council late on Saturday deplored the "brutal execution" of former president Najibullah, who was abducted by Taleban fighters from a U.N. compound on Friday where he had been given asylum.
Witnesses said the bodies of Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai, which had been strung from a tower in public view, had been removed overnight, but it was not known to where.

Holl declined to speak to reporters at Kabul airport, where he was met by a Taleban council member, Baz Mohammad, and protocol chief Mullah Hafeezullah. He was expected to convey the Security Council's protest against Najibullah's killing.
Afghanistan has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.

Najibullah led a Moscow-backed government for six years until he was ousted in 1992 by Moslem Mujahedeen, who refused to let him leave the country. He lived behind the walls of the U.N. headquarters in Kabul until his abduction.

The Security Council said in a statement it was "concerned at the violation of the United Nations premises in Kabul and expresses dismay at the brutal execution by the Taleban of the former president of Afghanistan, Najibullah, and others who had taken refuge in these premises."
The statement, read at a formal meeting, otherwise refrained from criticising the radical Islamic militia directly for its takeover of Kabul.

It expressed "grave concern" about the military confrontation, called for an immediate end to fighting and asked all Afghan leaders "to renounce the use of force, to put aside their differences and to engage in a political dialogue."

The Taleban has concentrated on consolidating its hold over the capital where it set up a strict fundamentalist Moslem government soon after capturing the city with little bloodshed at the climax of a sweep through eastern Afghanistan.

A Pakistan-based private Afghan news service said the Taleban had seized Charikar, capital of Parwan province north of Kabul, and were heading further north towards the Jabal-us-Seraj base of pro-Rabbani forces.

But reporters visiting the area said Rabbani's forces still controlled Charikar and Taleban fighters were making no attempt to advance from the Bagram military air base, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.

Four tanks flying Taleban's plain white flag guarded the edge of the militia's territory at Bagram. A score of Rabbani fighters manned a checkpoint just south of Charikar about 10 km (six miles) further north.
Rabbani has called on the world not to recognise the fundamentalist Islamic government decreed by Taleban, which said women should not report into work and promised death for adulterers and drinkers.
